title: `to_uppercase`, `to_lowercase`: Rust's Unicode mappings
description: Case mapping is Rust's `str::to_uppercase` and `to_lowercase`: full Unicode mappings, which can change the length (`ß` is `SS`, `İ` lowercases to `i̇`), with a final sigma (`ΣΑΣ` lowercases to `σας`). On ASCII they agree with the reference on every probe row.
reference: `upper`, `lower` with `char_set: UTF8`, a black box defined as Rust's `str::to_uppercase` (`Text.upper`); Lean evaluates them on ASCII only.

provenance.checked_by: D51 facts (C1 of the ruling on the raise sets)

evidence.note: `to_lowercase_helper`: the ASCII prefix byte by byte, then each `char` through `char::to_lowercase`, with `Σ` alone read in its context (`map_uppercase_sigma`); `to_uppercase` is the same without the sigma rule. Polars inlines std's `str::to_lowercase` / `to_uppercase`, so the mapping is scalar by scalar and the Σ is the one context rule

every Unicode scalar value (without surrogates) through `upper` and `lower` alone: 1580 values for `upper` and 1488 for `lower`; full mappings, and a final sigma (`lower('ΑΣ')` is `ας`); the context strings of `CONTEXT` are in the file's `context`

the values the three tier-1 engines map differently: 157 for `upper`, 56 for `lower` (213 in all, none in both); Polars and Spark agree on every one-character string, so each is DuckDB's simple mapping against their full one, and the final sigma is a context rule apart from them

provenance.notes: `sverify_dev.probe_polars` runs each expression on edge cases (0, ±1, ±2, 3, ±7, the bounds of the integer width; 0.5, ±2.5, 7, 1e308, ±inf, NaN; NULL), one row at a time, and compares each row with Lean's outcome of the Substrait call under each candidate option (`substrait-check --outcomes`). Observations are Polars programs whose result is recorded as it is. Polars 2.1.0 (Python), Rust crates at tag py-2.1.0 (commit 7f902bd3), on macOS arm64.

notes: Streaming gives what in memory gives on every probe and observation cited here.

`python -m sverify_dev.probe_polars --diff --write` runs each probe one row at a time and on a 6000-row column with `collect(engine='in-memory')` and `collect(engine='streaming')`, and each observation twice: its `df(...)` frame's `select`, `with_columns`, `filter`, `sort`, `unique`, `join` and `group_by` go through the streaming engine the second time (`StreamingFrame`); the `s-` observations collect a lazy query on each engine themselves. Polars 2.1.0 (Python), macOS arm64.
